To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a multivariate frequency-domain analysis can be used to identify and forecast long-term oscillatory climatic modes.

the paradigm of a stochastic system with a small number of quasi-oscillation modes superposed on a stochastic noise background is consistent with observed climatic data, and that a multivariate frequency-domain methodology is a particularly effective means by which to identify and forecast the quasi-oscillations.
the paradigm of a quasi-oscillating climate system with characteristic modes and a stochastic background noise can be used to develop effective long-lead climatological forecasting techniques.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a new approach to the detection of coherent spatiotempory patterns of variability in the climate system, and with the development of a new forecasting methodology that is guided by the detection of such patterns.
developing a multivariate frequency-domain framework for the analysis, prediction, and detection of long-lead climate signals.
the development and evaluation of new methods for long-range climatic forecast.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a paradigm shift is needed in the way we view climate variability.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the paradigm of a stochastic climate system with a finite number of spatiotem-poral modes of variability can lead to a more effective approach to long-range climatic prediction.
the proposed approach can be applied in the context of any climate system that exhibits quasi-oscillations and noise.
a frequency-domain approach can be a powerful tool in the detection and forecasting of spatiotemperatureally organized climatic signals.
